title: Validating SQL: containment, provers, refutation
objective: Validate generated SQL per command against the source, replay every counterexample through both semantics, and stamp "results match on one database" as [T] · 1 instance.

blocks.md: Your compiler turns each command into SQL, and an agent offers a faster rewrite of one statement. Your suite agrees with it. This lesson is about what that agreement establishes, and about checking the compiler's output one command at a time instead.

choice.prompt: An agent rewrote your compiled credit as an upsert, `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE`. The fixture database and your S6 suite agree with the original. What is established?

options.why: Agreement on instances is a test.

options.text: It agrees on the instances tried: TESTED [T] · 1 instance for the fixture.
options.why: One instance is evidence, stamped as such.

options.text: It is equivalent whenever the accounts exist.
options.why: The instances tried are read as all the relevant ones, and the schema allows a missing account.
A matching instance is evidence, and the stamp says how much.

blocks.md:
The validator compares outcome classes for each command: a commit with balances related by your R(S, D), a typed error, or a database error code. Evidence for a verdict comes in three kinds, and each earns its own stamp.

| Evidence | Tools, on your Bench | Stamp |
|---|---|---|
| A proof for a fragment | containment by homomorphism (drawer D-17), QED | [P] of the prover's encoding, uncertified |
| A bounded search | VeriEQL, databases up to a size | [M] · bound |
| Refutation and tests | Polygon, generated databases | [R] after replay, otherwise [T] · n |

A prover's NEQ is not [R]: only an instance that replays through both semantics refutes. A model's "equivalent" earns no stamp at all.
The original credit and the upsert, on a database that lacks the destination account. On the fixture database, where account 2 exists, the two agree.
blocks.direction: Read the row count each statement reports, then the table. In your plan, a credit that touches zero rows becomes a typed error and a rollback.

call.prompt: On a database that lacks the destination account, what happens?

options.why: An upsert inserts the row when none matches, so it does not fail.
The UPDATE matches no row and reports `UPDATE 0` {{run:RUN-pg-one-db}}, and the plan's rowcount check rolls it back.

options.text: The original rolls back with a typed error. The upsert creates the account and commits.
options.why: One statement reports zero rows, the other inserts one.

blocks.after: The credit reported `UPDATE 0`, which your plan turns into a typed error and a rollback. The upsert reported `INSERT 0 1` and left account 2 at 30 {{run:RUN-pg-one-db}}. On the fixture both leave account 2 at 80, so your suite saw nothing. This is SP-9.4, an erosion: SEAM-11 cracks, and CL-6.1's correspondence held only for the one instance it tried.

blocks.md: Restate CL-6.1 from memory: your suite's agreement says the compiler's SQL means what your commands mean. Its strip has three segments: the proposition of the model, the correspondence between model and database, and the requirement fit.

choice.prompt: A rewrite agrees with the original on your fixture and differs on a database without the destination account. Which segment of CL-6.1's strip cracks?

options.why: The source semantics did not change. The rewrite is not what it describes.
One database's agreement stood for the compiler, and a second database disagrees.
The requirement is unchanged. What broke is the link from model to database.
A passing suite is the evidence that missed it.

blocks.md: A shape check is the cheap alternative to a replay. Here is a mutant of the compiled transfer whose credit names the source account.

blocks.direction: The reference validator runs both checks on the plan, from a fixture where accounts 1 and 2 hold 100 and 0.

code.text:
plan    transfer 30 from account 1 to account 2, with the credit naming account 1
  UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 30 WHERE id = 1 AND bal >= 30    -- expects 1 row
  UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 30 WHERE id = 1                  -- expects 1 row

check   shape      two UPDATEs, each WHERE id = <parameter>, each expecting one row
check   semantic   lift both sides to IR form, compare outcome classes, replay any rejection

call.prompt: Does the shape check accept the mutant?

options.why: The shape is intact: two UPDATEs, each by id, each touching one row.
A shape check cannot see which account a parameter names.

blocks.after: The shape check accepts it. The semantic check rejects it with an instance that replays: account 2 never receives the 30 {{run:RUN-sql-shape-validator}}. This is SP-9.2. The validator you build replays each plan on PGlite and the source on the interpreter, and rejects only with an instance whose outcome classes differ.

blocks.md: A counterexample must satisfy the schema, here `bal bigint NOT NULL CHECK (bal >= 0)`. An instance the database cannot insert is spurious and is discarded.

choice.prompt: A guard in your plan reads `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT acct_id FROM holds)`. The agent rewrites it as `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM holds h WHERE h.acct_id = acct.id)`, and `holds.acct_id` allows NULL. Which schema-valid instance separates them?

options.why: Both guards let every account through, so they agree.
Both guards stop account 1 and let the others through.

options.text: `holds` has one row whose `acct_id` is NULL.
options.why: `id NOT IN (…, NULL)` is never true, so the original lets no account through. `NOT EXISTS` finds no match and lets them all through.
The CHECK refuses that row. An instance the database cannot insert is spurious.

choice.prompt: A bounded checker finds no counterexample among all databases of up to 4 rows per table. Which stamp does the pair earn?

options.why: A bound limits the search. Databases of 5 rows were never tried.

options.text: MODEL-CHECKED [M] · up to 4 rows per table
options.why: Every database within the bound was checked, and the bound is part of the stamp.
It searched every database up to the bound, not one.
The search finished, and a stamp that names its bound is available.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: Singh and Bedathur, arXiv 2412.05561 (v2, 2025-06-08), on how LLM judges decide query equivalence, and Chandra and Merlin, STOC 1977, on containment, with drawer D-17 beside it.

blocks.title: Build this
blocks.md: LAB-9.11 asks for the validator: it lifts each statement to IR form, compares outcome classes, and replays every rejection on both semantics.

RUN-pg-one-db.title: PostgreSQL 18.6: the compiled credit and the upsert agree on the fixture database; without the destination row the credit updates 0 rows and the upsert inserts account 2

values.server: PostgreSQL 18.6 (Debian 18.6-1.pgdg13+2) on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu, compiled by gcc (Debian 14.2.0-19) 14.2.0, 64-bit

notes: Recorded by W1 follow-up 1 (task_label W1-followup-1); the task field is left out because run@1 accepts only W<n>-S<nn> or W<n>-T<nn> there.

Each configuration ran in its own fresh server: docker run -d of postgres:18@sha256:74935e72241653ca55e0414067e6d8763aceb8a810eb51b452253ec3dcfc4336 with --network none, --memory=6g and trust authentication, the work directory mounted read-only at /q; the recorder waited until docker logs showed "PostgreSQL init process complete" and "database system is ready to accept connections" twice and pg_isready exited 0 (at most 120 polls, 0.5 s apart), then ran psql through docker exec and sh with stdout and stderr merged by 2>&1, so the log is in the order psql wrote it, and removed the container. argv lists the commands in order (start, prelude when there is one, psql, removal); started_at, duration_s and exit_code are the psql command's. psql ran with -X and -v VERBOSITY=verbose, so each ERROR line carries its SQLSTATE; the SQL files ran unchanged, several -f files in one psql session.

In the cell the statements run outside a transaction, as the lesson's cell does: the plan's rowcount check (a 0-row credit becomes NoSuchAccount and a rollback) is the lesson's reading of `UPDATE 0`, not something this script executes. values.missing_row holds the two command tags and the final table; values.fixture holds each credit's tag and the table it left before its rollback.
